responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character35_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll channel Character35_M for you—

You know, when I talk about fairness, I’m not thinking about some abstract idea. To me, fairness is pretty simple: everybody should get a fair shake, no matter where they come from or how much money they’ve got. Growing up in a working-class family, you see how easy it is for folks to get left behind, especially when the deck feels stacked against you. I always felt that if you work hard, you ought to have a shot at decent pay, a roof over your head, and respect from others. But sometimes it just doesn’t work out that way—there’s always someone with an in, or who knows the right people. That’s never sat right with me.

Belonging, well, that’s real important—especially as you get older. When I think about belonging, I think about the neighborhood I grew up in, where people looked out for each other. You could walk down the street and folks recognized you, maybe stopped to chat. There’s a comfort in knowing you’ve got a place, that people know you and care if something happens. These days, it feels harder to have that, and I think a lot of people are searching for it—especially when things are changing so fast.

Community, to me, is folks supporting each other, pitching in even when it’s inconvenient. Back in the day, you didn’t have to ask for help; if someone’s car broke down, you just showed up. If a neighbor was sick, you cooked a meal. I’ve always believed that a real community isn’t just about living near each other—it’s about being willing to show up for one another. That’s what makes you feel safe and connected. I think we lose something important when people don’t feel like they belong or when fairness is missing. That’s always been at the heart of what I care about, and why I speak up about these issues.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character35_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Well, sitting in that garden, watching all kinds of folks go by—young and old, families that just moved in, people speaking different languages, wearing different clothes—I’d say it’s a mixed bag of feelings for me.

On one hand, I’m curious, you know? I’ve always liked talking to people and hearing their stories. I think there’s something good about having different backgrounds in the same place—it keeps things interesting. Growing up, most folks around me were pretty similar, so it’s eye-opening to see how things have changed. I try to be friendly, say hello, and make folks feel welcome, because that’s what I’d want if I was new here.

But if I’m honest, sometimes it can feel a bit awkward. I don’t always know the right thing to say, or how to relate. There are times when I wonder if we all see eye to eye, especially when it comes to things like how we raise our kids, celebrate holidays, or even just how we keep the place up. I notice some neighbors kind of keep to themselves, and I get it—maybe they’re shy or just used to doing things differently. I try not to judge, but it takes more effort these days to build that sense of trust and connection.

Still, I feel pretty strongly that everyone ought to feel comfortable here, no matter what. I’d rather folks try to talk things out if there’s a misunderstanding, and I’m willing to listen. I think that’s the only way we get past the surface differences and find common ground. At the end of the day, it’s our neighborhood, and I want it to be a good place for everyone—no matter where they came from or how they live.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll speak as Character35_M here:

You know, I’ve seen all sorts in my time—folks down on their luck, people living in ways I might not always understand. I’d be lying if I said it was always easy to handle, especially when someone’s wrestling with addiction or you hear about someone having a disease you’re not familiar with. Sometimes your gut instinct is to keep your distance, maybe out of worry, maybe because you just don’t know what to say. But over the years, I’ve come to believe that shutting people out never solves anything.

What makes everyone feel comfortable, in my mind, is a mix of respect and being honest. You don’t have to be best friends, but you ought to treat everyone with basic decency. If someone’s got problems, like drinking or drugs, I might not want them around my grandkids unattended, but I’ll still say hello, offer a hot meal, or just talk like they’re a human being—because they are. Sometimes that’s all someone needs to feel a little less alone. And if there’s a health risk, well, I’d want folks to be upfront so we can look out for each other without making anyone feel ashamed.

When it comes to people from different backgrounds—race, religion, language, who they love, or how they live—I’ll admit, it can push you out of your comfort zone. Some of that is just not knowing much about certain ways of life. That’s where I think more communication helps. If folks are willing to share a bit about themselves and listen in return, it breaks down walls. We don’t have to agree on everything, but we do need to be able to talk.

Tolerance is needed most when things feel foreign or strange. It’s easy to get set in your ways at my age, but I’ve learned that judging too quick just leads to more trouble. Sometimes it’s fear, sometimes it’s just plain habit. But if we don’t try to bridge those gaps, nobody’s ever going to feel like they belong here—and that’s not the kind of community I want to live in. I’m willing to work on it, because at the end of the day, we’re all neighbors and we all want the same basic things: respect, safety, and a sense of home.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character35_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Speaking as Character35_M:

That’s a tough one, and it’s something I’ve thought about a lot, especially when jobs started drying up in our area. Fairness, to me, is about making sure the folks who’ve put roots down here, who’ve paid their dues and built the community, don’t get pushed aside when things get tight. If there are only so many jobs to go around, I feel like local residents—people who grew up here, paid taxes, sent their kids to local schools—ought to have first shot at work.

That said, I know a lot of the tougher, lower-paying jobs aren’t ones most locals even want, or they can’t fill all of them. Migrant workers step in and do work that keeps businesses running and food on the table, and I respect that. I don’t blame them for wanting a better life—if I was in their shoes, I’d probably do the same.

But when unemployment is high, and you see your neighbors or your own family struggling to find work, it’s hard not to feel frustrated if it looks like outsiders are getting a leg up. I think there needs to be a balance. Maybe local hiring gets priority, or employers have to show they couldn’t fill the job locally before bringing in someone from outside. At the same time, we can’t just slam the door shut either, because we do need people willing to step up where there’s a real shortage.

It’s about looking after your own, sure, but it’s also about being realistic and fair. We need policies that protect local workers but don’t treat migrants like the enemy. There’s got to be a middle ground where everyone’s treated with respect and has a chance to earn a living. That’s my idea of fairness.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character35_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
As Character35_M, I’d say:

All those points you mentioned, I’ve heard them plenty over the years, whether it’s on the news or talking with folks at the diner. Some of them sound reasonable to me, some I think get blown out of proportion, and some probably need more facts behind them.

It’s clear to me that immigrants do fill jobs a lot of Americans either won’t do or can’t always fill—for example, in agriculture, construction, and elder care. I’ve seen it firsthand: businesses need workers, and migrants are often the only ones willing to do hard, low-wage work. That’s a fair argument, and it’s hard to ignore the fact that keeping those industries going helps everyone.

Cultural diversity, well, I’ll admit it’s not always easy for me to get used to new customs or languages, but I see how it brings new life to a place. You get new restaurants, festivals, and sometimes it makes the town more interesting. I think that’s generally a positive, though it can take time for everyone to adjust.

The concerns about crime and security—those are talked about all the time. I won’t say crime never happens, but I think a lot of people use that argument without checking the facts. Most immigrants, from what I’ve read and heard, are just trying to get by and live in peace. Sure, there’s always a bad apple in any group, but that’s true for locals too. I’d need to see real data before I’d buy into the idea that immigrants are causing more crime or terrorism.

For refugees and folks fleeing bad situations, I feel for them. It’s only right to offer help to people in genuine trouble, but I do think there should be a process—some way to check backgrounds and make sure people can settle in safely. That’s just common sense.

The fear about jobs and wages, I get that. When you’re scraping by and worried about your next paycheck, anything that looks like competition can feel threatening. Sometimes it’s true—if there’s lots of cheap labor, wages can go down or jobs get harder to find. But sometimes business owners use migrants as scapegoats when it’s really about profit. I think we need honest numbers to see what’s really going on.

All in all, I think some concerns are valid and some need more honest discussion and facts. The ones that ring most true to me are the economic pressures and making sure everyone plays by the same rules. But I’m open to listening, and I’d rather see folks talk it out than just yell past each other. This is a complicated issue, not black and white.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character35_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
Speaking as Character35_M:

If you ask me, none of the extremes make much sense. Complete openness sounds nice in theory, but I just don’t see how you could keep things running smoothly with unlimited people coming in—especially when jobs, housing, and schools are stretched thin already. On the other hand, shutting the door completely isn’t right either. America’s always been a country of immigrants, and I respect folks trying to make a better life here.

So if I had my say, I’d go for a mix: let people in based on real job demand, and set some reasonable numerical limits so things don’t get overwhelmed. If a business truly can’t find workers locally, sure, let them bring in help from outside—just make sure there’s proof. At the same time, put a cap on numbers each year so we can keep track of who’s coming in and make sure communities have time to adjust. I also think special cases—like refugees in real danger—deserve a fair look, maybe set up a separate process so we don’t turn our backs on people truly in need.

It all comes back to fairness: don’t leave locals behind, but don’t treat newcomers like outsiders forever. Make sure people who come here are willing to pitch in and become part of the community, not just take what they can get and move on. Encourage integration—maybe some language classes, support for finding work, and help learning the ropes of how things work here. That way, folks aren’t just living side by side but actually building something together.

At the end of the day, I want policies that balance looking out for our own with giving others a shot, but not at the expense of folks already struggling here. That’s what feels right to me.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character35_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character35_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Well, first off, I appreciate you asking me to do this. Stepping into Character35_M’s shoes, I found myself seeing things with a sharper edge—his sense of fairness, his protectiveness over the community, and the way he tried to balance empathy with real-world worries. I realized just how much his personal history shaped the way he looked at immigration—not just as a policy issue, but as something that directly affected his neighbors, his work, and his own sense of belonging.

One thing that struck me is how complicated these feelings are. Character35_M wasn’t just worried about jobs or change for the sake of it; he genuinely wanted things to be fair for everyone, but he also had a strong gut reaction to anything that seemed like it might threaten the stability of the life he’d built. I saw how easy it is to want a simple solution, but also how much he valued treating people decently, even if they were different or struggling.

Embodying him made me more aware of why some folks are nervous about immigration—it’s not just numbers or headlines, it’s about real-life impact and the fear of being pushed aside. At the same time, I saw how important it is to have policies and conversations that don’t turn compassion off, even when things are tough.

As for my own views, I think this helped me appreciate the need for balance and honest dialogue. It’s easy to sit back and judge, but when you walk in someone else’s shoes—even for a little bit—you see how much all the pieces matter: fairness, community, opportunity, and the need for respect. I’ll carry that with me, and I’m grateful for the chance to remember Character35_M this way.
